title: Why Do You Want This Internship? How to Answer (With Examples)
summary: A three-part reply that fits in under a minute, weak vs. strong samples for tech, finance and consulting, plus how to adapt it for "why are you interested in this position."
body_markdown:
Answer it in three parts, in this order: what you want to learn, why this team or company and not another one, and what you will bring to the team this summer. Keep it to about 45 to 60 seconds out loud, or 100 to 150 words on an application. Name one specific thing about the company that you could not have said about its competitor.


Most weak answers miss that last part. I read a lot of answers to this question, and the weak ones are interchangeable: swap the company name and nothing else changes. The strong ones could only have been written for one internship.


## The three-part answer


Part What it answers What to include Length


**1. What you want to learn** Why this kind of internship One skill or kind of work you want to get better at, tied to a class, project or job you have done 1 to 2 sentences


**2. Why this company** Why here and not somewhere else One specific fact: a product, a team, a deal, a program, something an employee told you 1 to 2 sentences


**3. What you bring** Why they should pick you One thing you have already done that shows you can do the work 1 to 2 sentences


Here is a full example for a software engineering internship. It is made up, but every part of it is the kind of detail you can find in an hour of research:


> "I want to spend the summer working on a product that a lot of people use every day, because my projects so far have only had a few users. Your team's post about moving checkout to a new payments system caught my attention, because I built a small payments flow for a campus club app last spring and ran into the same retry problem you described. I'd bring that experience, plus two semesters as a TA for our data structures course, where I got used to explaining code clearly."


It is about 85 words and takes roughly 40 seconds to say.


## Weak vs. strong answers


Weak Why it falls flat Strong


"I've always admired your company." Says nothing you could not say about any company "I've used your budgeting app since freshman year, and the new shared-accounts feature is the first one I've recommended to my roommates."


"It would be a great learning opportunity." True of every internship "I want to learn how a team decides what to build next. In my projects, I've always been the one person deciding."


"Your company is a leader in the industry." Sounds copied from the About page "You're one of the few banks in my city with a restructuring group that takes summer analysts."


"I need an internship for my degree." Honest, but about you, not them "My program requires an internship, and I chose yours because the rotation lets me try two teams before I pick a track."


"I'm passionate about technology." Every candidate says it "I spent last summer building a tool to track my club's events, and I want to see how that kind of work scales."


## Examples by field


### Tech or software engineering


Focus on the product and the engineering work. Mention something real: a feature, a public engineering blog post, an open source project, or a talk an engineer gave. Then connect it to a project of your own.


> "I want to get better at building things that run at scale. Your team's write-up on cutting page load time for the mobile app is the kind of problem I'd like to work on, and I did a smaller version of it when I rebuilt my school's course-search site to load twice as fast."


### Finance (investment banking, sales and trading)


Focus on the group, the kind of deals or clients, and the office. Banks expect you to know why their bank and why this division. A recent deal from the firm's press releases works well, as long as you can talk about it if they follow up.


> "I want to learn how deals are built from the first model to the close. Your healthcare group advised on two hospital mergers this year, and I'm interested in healthcare after working at a clinic for two summers. In my finance club I've built three-statement models for case competitions, so I'd come in knowing the basics and ready to learn the rest."


### Consulting


Focus on the type of problems the firm works on and how it trains interns. Firms want to hear that you like structured problem solving and working with clients.


> "I want to learn how to break a messy business problem into pieces a team can actually solve. I talked to two of your consultants at our career fair, and both mentioned that interns lead a workstream instead of just supporting one. I've done that on a smaller scale as project lead for a student consulting group, where we helped a local nonprofit cut its volunteer no-show rate."


## On a written application


Many applications ask some version of this question in a text box. The same three parts work, in 100 to 150 words:


1. Open with what you want to learn, in one sentence.
2. Give the one specific reason for this company.
3. End with what you bring, with one result or number if you have it.


Write a new answer for each company. Simplify users have submitted more than 200 million applications with Copilot, and if you are applying to many internships, Simplify's free[Copilot](https://simplify.jobs/copilot?utm_source=blog&utm_medium=cta&utm_campaign=why-do-you-want-this-internship&utm_content=written-answer) fills the repeated parts of the form (contact details, education, work history) so your time goes to answers like this one. With Simplify+, it can also draft a first version from the job description and your resume. Edit that draft until the specific reason is yours.


## "Why do you want to work here?" and "Why are you interested in this position?"


These are the same question for full-time roles, and the same three parts work. Shift the weight a little:


- **Why do you want to work here?** Lead with part 2, the company. Interviewers asking this want to know you will stay.
- **Why are you interested in this position?** Lead with part 1, the work itself, then connect it to what you have done before.
- **Why this internship over others you applied to?** It is fine to admit you applied to several. Say what makes this one your first choice, and keep it specific.


## Mistakes to avoid


- **Talking about salary, location or perks first.** They can matter to you, but they should not be your main reason.
- **Reciting the mission statement.** The interviewer wrote it, or at least has read it many times.
- **Going over two minutes.** If you are still talking after a minute, stop at the end of part 3.
- **Naming a fact you cannot discuss.** If you mention a deal or a product, be ready for a follow-up question about it.
- **Using the same answer everywhere.** Interviewers can tell, and so can anyone reading two of your applications side by side.


## Common questions


**How long should my answer to "why do you want this internship" be?** About 45 to 60 seconds out loud, or 100 to 150 words written. Three short parts are enough: what you want to learn, why this company and what you bring.


**What if I don't know much about the company?** Spend 30 minutes before the interview. Read the careers page for the internship, one recent news story or press release, and one post or talk by someone on the team. One specific detail is enough.


**Can I say I want the internship to get a full-time offer?** Yes, briefly. Saying you hope to come back full time shows you are serious, but it should not be your only reason. Pair it with what you want to learn there.


**Is "why do you want this internship" the same as "why do you want to work here"?** Close. The internship version is more about what you want to learn; the general version is more about the company. Use the same three parts and change which one comes first.


**Should I memorize my answer?** Memorize the three points, not the exact words. A memorized script sounds flat, and you will lose your place if they interrupt.


## Find internships worth a specific answer


Simplify lists thousands of open internships, and in a 2022 survey of Harvard CS students it ranked among the top three places they found tech internships ([Harvard career center, archived](https://web.archive.org/web/20240228134502/https://careerservices.fas.harvard.edu/blog/2022/11/22/beyond-big-tech-where-can-i-find-summer-opportunities/) ).
